title: Contra Julianum
author: Augustine
source: Translated by Claude from tmp747.tmp747.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

passages.original: 6. Multo autem apertius de eadem fide4 beatissimus martyr et episcopus Cyprianus: < Si homines, > inquit, < impedire aliquid ad consecutionem graiix1 posset, magis adultos et provectos et majores natu possent impedire peccata graviora. Porro autem si gravissimis delictoribus ei in Deum multum ante peccantibus, cum postea crediderint, remissa0 peccatorum datur, et a Baptismo atque gratia nemo prohibetur; quanto magis prohiberi non debet infans, qui recens natus nihil peccavit, nisi quod secundum Adam carnaliter natus, contagium mortis antiquae prima nativitate contraxit?
passages.english: 6. But the most blessed martyr and bishop Cyprian [speaks] much more plainly about the same faith: "If anything," he says, "could hinder men from obtaining grace, it is rather the graver sins that could hinder adults, the advanced and those older in years. But if remission of sins is granted even to the most grievous offenders, who have sinned much against God beforehand, when afterwards they have believed, and no one is barred from Baptism and grace, how much more ought an infant not to be barred, who, newly born, has committed no sin, except that, being born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of the ancient death by his first birth?"
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: 'graiix1' read as 'gratiae', 'remissa0' as 'remissa', 'ei' as 'et'; '4' is a footnote mark. 'Si homines' is evidently a corruption of 'si homines aliquid', i.e. 'if anything could hinder men'; translated accordingly.

passages.original: Sed numquid, « infantes etiamsi Don baptizentur, habere vitam aeternam, > ulla callidilate in aliud detorquere, vel ullis foliis ficulneis operire potuistis? Eos enim qui hoc dicunt, non po. tuit apud catholicos judices nisi damnare Pelagius : et quod sentiebat, damnavit coram bominibus, damnarimetuensabhominibus. Namsi hoc non sentitis, nobis utique consentitis. Sed quia nobis non consentitis, illud sine dubitatione sentitis. Ac per hoc orientales vos judices damnant *, a quibus Pelagius damnari timens, eos qui sentiunt ista damnavit, cum eis quos damnavit profecto damnandus, quia id quod negavit ore, corde servavit.
passages.english: But were you able, by any cunning, to twist into another sense, or to cover with any fig leaves, [the statement] "that infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life"? For Pelagius could do nothing before catholic judges but condemn those who say this; and what he held, he condemned in the presence of men, fearing to be condemned by men. For if you do not hold this, you certainly agree with us. But since you do not agree with us, you hold that [view] without any doubt. And for this reason the eastern judges condemn you, those by whom Pelagius, fearing to be condemned, condemned those who hold these things, though he himself certainly deserves to be condemned along with those whom he condemned, because what he denied with his mouth he kept in his heart.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected silently (e.g. 'Don' for 'non', 'callidilate' for 'calliditate', run-together words 'damnarimetuensabhominibus. Namsi'). The asterisk after 'damnant' is an editorial mark and is omitted.

passages.original: en adest assertorum ejus memorabilis ct venerabilis, consessus atque consensus. Sanctus Irenæus. dicit, antiquam serpentis plagam fide Christi et cruce sanari, et quod protoplasti peccato ruimus tanquam vinculis alligati. Sanctus Cyprianus dicit, perire parvulum, nisi fuerit baptizatus, quamvis ei non propria dimittantur, sed aliena peccata. Sanctus Reticius dicit, vetcris hominis, quo per lavacrum regenerationis exuimur, non tantum vetera, sed ingenita esse peccata. Sanctus Olympius dicit, vilium de protoplasto iit germine sparsum, ut peccatum cum homine nascc. retur. Sanctus Hilarius dicit, ex pccoato essc omnem carnem, praeter illius, qui venit in similitudine caruis peccati sine peccato. Dicit, sub peccati origine et sub peccati leae natum esse, eujus vox est, Ego in iniquitatibus conceptus sum (Psal. L,7). Sanctus Ambrosius dicit, eos qui baptizati fueriut parvulos in priniordia natura suce a malitia reformari. Dicit, solum ex natis de femina sanctum Dominum Jesum, nulla terrenæ contagia corruptelæ immaculati partus novitate scnsissc.
passages.english: Here is present the memorable and venerable assembly and agreement of its defenders. Saint Irenaeus says that the ancient wound of the serpent is healed by faith in Christ and by the cross, and that through the sin of the first-formed man we fell as if bound with chains. Saint Cyprian says that a little child perishes unless he has been baptised, although it is not his own sins but another's that are forgiven him. Saint Reticius says that the sins of the old man, whom we put off through the washing of regeneration, are not only old but inborn. Saint Olympius says that the fault was spread from the first-formed man in the seed, so that sin was born with man. Saint Hilary says that all flesh is from sin, except the flesh of him who came in the likeness of sinful flesh without sin. He says that he whose voice says, "I was conceived in iniquities" (Ps. 50:7), was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin. Saint Ambrose says that those who have been baptised as little children are reformed from wickedness to the first beginnings of their nature. He says that alone of those born of woman the holy Lord Jesus, by the newness of his immaculate birth, felt no contagion of earthly corruption.
passages.notes: Many scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. 'vilium' = 'vitium', 'iit' = 'in', 'leae' = 'lege', 'priniordia natura suce' = 'primordia naturae suae'). The opening 'en' is likely the end of 'En' or a fragment ('Behold'). 'In the seed' renders 'in germine'.

passages.original: > Hæc clamas pro Manichæis contra vocem catholicæ veritatis per sacerdotem Dei prolatam ; ut si tu andiaris, Manichæi vincant, dicentes, ut alia taceam . « Si rerum ratio non sinit ut de bono malum aliquid proferatur; > non ergo ex bonis, sicut dicit Ambrosius, sed, sicut nos dicimus, ex mali natura orta sunt mala. Ecce in quantam voraginem decidisti male intelligendo Dominum dicentem , Arbor bona fructus malo non facit: cum hoc non sit dictum de natura, vel de nuptiis, quas instituit Deus, sed de voluntate hominis bona, a qua non fiunt opera mala.
passages.english: These things you cry out on behalf of the Manichees against the voice of catholic truth uttered through a priest of God, so that, if you are listened to, the Manichees win, saying, to pass over other things: "If the nature of things does not allow anything evil to be produced from good," then evils have not arisen from goods, as Ambrose says, but, as we say, from the nature of evil. See into what an abyss you have fallen by wrongly understanding the Lord when he says, "A good tree does not produce bad fruit": whereas this was not said about nature, or about marriage, which God instituted, but about the good will of a man, from which evil works do not come.

passages.original: etde natura quam facit Deus, ipsa quoe faciat fructus malos, nascitur arbur mala : quasi aliquid melius faciat homo, unde non possit malus fructus existere; quam est illud quod facit Deus, unde possit mala arbor existere ? ne quis ergo sic erret, audiat diligenter Ambrosium dicentem, f Quid est malitia, nisi boni indigentia ? Non enim sunt mala nisi quæ privantur bonis; quia indigentia boni, radix malitiæ est. > Et hinc intelligat ideo esse arborem malam, voluntatem malam; quia defectus est a summo bono, ubi bonum creatum bono creante privatur, ut sit in eo radix mali nihil aliud qnam iinligentia boni.
passages.english: and that from the nature which God makes, which itself would produce bad fruits, a bad tree is born: as though man makes something better, from which bad fruit cannot come forth, than what God makes, from which a bad tree can come forth? So that no one may err in this way, let him listen carefully to Ambrose saying: "What is wickedness but the lack of good? For there are no evils except things deprived of goods; because the lack of good is the root of wickedness." And from this let him understand that the bad tree is the bad will precisely because it is a falling away from the highest good, where the created good is deprived of the creating good, so that the root of evil in it is nothing other than the lack of good.
passages.notes: Continues a sentence begun in the preceding context ('lest someone say, How is it that from the tree man makes ... no bad fruits come'). Scanning errors corrected ('arbur', 'qnam iinligentia').

passages.original: Nec ista quinque argumenta vestra, ex quibus cuncta connectitis, quæ in hac quæstione adversus catholicam fidem multipliciter disputatis, singillatim testimoniis sanctorum refutanda suscipiam : sed quantum potuerit eorum percuti et dejici, etiam cnm a me de litteris catholicorum episcoporum singula proferentur, tantum percutietur atque dejicietur, sive unum eorum, sive duo, sivc plura, sive omnia, sicut valuerit quod proferetur. Veluti est iI- lud in libro quom de Arca Noe conscripsit beatas Ambrosius, « Per unum, i inquit, < Dominum Je-sum salus ventura nationibus declaratur, qui solus non potuit justus essc 1, cum generatio omnis erraret, nisi natus ex virginc generationis obnoxiæ privilegio minime tcnerclur. Ecce, inquit, in iniquitatibus conceptus sun, et in delictis peperit me mater mea (Psal. L, 7), dicit is qui justus præ cæteris putabatur.
passages.english: Nor shall I undertake to refute one by one with testimonies of the saints those five arguments of yours, from which you link together everything that you argue in many ways on this question against the catholic faith; but as far as any of them can be struck and overthrown, even when I bring forward individual passages from the writings of catholic bishops, so far it will be struck and overthrown, whether one of them, or two, or more, or all, according to the force of what is brought forward. Such is that passage in the book which blessed Ambrose wrote on Noah's Ark: "Through the one Lord Jesus," he says, "salvation is declared to be coming to the nations, who alone could not have been righteous, since every generation went astray, unless, being born of a virgin, he was in no way held by the privilege of a guilty generation. 'Behold,' he says, 'I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother bore me' (Ps. 50:7): so says he who was thought righteous beyond others."
passages.notes: 'Privilegio' here seems to mean 'binding law/condition' of guilty birth rather than 'privilege'; translated literally.

passages.original: 6. Denique dicit etiam victoriosissimus Cyprianus in epistola sua de Oratione dominica : i Fieri autem petimus voluntatem Dei in cœlo et in terra : quod utrumque ad consummationem nostrae incolumitatis pertinet et salutis. Nam cum corpus e terra, et spiritum possideamus c cœlo, ipsi terra et cœlum sumus, et in utroque, id est in corpore et in spiritu, ut Dei voluntas fiat oramus. Est enim inter carnem et spiritum colluctatio, et discordantibus adversus se invicem quotidiana congressio, ut non quæ volumus ipsa faciamus;
passages.english: 6. Finally, the most victorious Cyprian too says in his letter on the Lord's Prayer: "We ask that the will of God be done in heaven and on earth: both of which pertain to the completion of our safety and salvation. For since we possess the body from earth and the spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven, and in both, that is, in body and in spirit, we pray that God's will be done. For there is a struggle between the flesh and the spirit, and a daily conflict between them as they are at odds with one another, so that we do not do the very things we will;

passages.original: Sed ne forte dicas, contra hoc potius pugnare baptizatos, quod sibi ipsi prioris vitas mala consuetudine fecerunt, non contra id cum quo nati sunt: quanquam si hoc dicis, jam procul dubio ceruis atque concedis, esse in homine aliquid mali, quod non ipsum, sed reatus qui ex illo contractus fuerat, auferatur in Baptismo : tamen quia parlim est ad hujus quaestionis absolutionem , nisi nobis ex peccato primi hominis ingeneratum esse monstrctur, audi quid inde in alio loco expressius dicat sanctus Ambrosius in expositione Evangelii secundum Lucam, cum diversis modis, ab una tamen regula fidei non abhorrentibus, tractaret illum locum, ubi Dominus ait, in una domo dividi tres adversus duos, et duos adversus tres 1 (Luc.
passages.english: But lest you perhaps say that the baptised fight rather against what they made for themselves by the bad habit of their former life, not against that with which they were born — although if you say this, you already without doubt see and grant that there is something evil in man which is not itself removed in Baptism, but the guilt that had been contracted from it — yet because it contributes little to the settling of this question unless it is shown to us to have been inborn from the sin of the first man, hear what Saint Ambrose says more explicitly on this point in another place, in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke, when he was treating in various ways, yet not departing from the one rule of faith, that passage where the Lord says that in one house three will be divided against two, and two against three (Luke
passages.notes: 'ceruis' read as 'cernis'; 'parlim' read as 'parum'.

passages.original: > Et in quibusdam locis sensus meos ad tuum potius interpretaris arbitrium, abutens tardiusculis cordibus hominum, qui le non intelligunt tacere po* lius noluisse, quan respondere potuissc uni meo, quatuor voluminibus tuis. Ecce fundit eloquentiæ lucidum ac perspicuum numen Ambrosius: non est ubi hae- I reat lector, ubi caliget auditor. Manifestissime dicit Apostolum ideo dixisse, Quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus?quia quia omnes sub peccato nascimur, et ipse ortus in vitio est. Manifestissime dicit, Dominum Christum propterca fuisse sine peccato, quod natus ex virgine vinculis obnoxiæ generationis naturaeque communis minime teneretur, et damnasse peccatum quod nascendo non sensit.
passages.english: And in certain places you interpret my meaning rather according to your own will, abusing the rather slow hearts of men, who do not understand that you would rather not have been silent than been able to answer my single [book] with your four volumes. See, Ambrose pours forth the clear and transparent light of eloquence: there is no place where the reader may get stuck, where the hearer may be in the dark. He says most plainly that the Apostle said, "Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" because we are all born under sin, and our very origin is in fault. He says most plainly that Christ the Lord was without sin for this reason, that, born of a virgin, he was in no way held by the chains of a guilty generation and common nature, and that he condemned the sin which he did not experience in being born.
passages.notes: 'numen' probably a misreading of 'lumen' (light). The clause about 'not wishing to be silent rather than being able to answer' is condensed; sense: Julian preferred to speak at length rather than truly answer. 'quia quia' is a duplication.

passages.original: Iste repugnantis impetus si laxetur, in quæ declinabit immunda? in quae non pertrahet et præcipitabit abrupta ? Verum nunc, quod potius instat, ecce non secundum vos quicumque Judaeus, sed secundum beatum Ambrosium de se ipso Paulus apostolus dicit, Video aliam legem in membris meis, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, et captivantem mf in lege peccati. Rursus in eodem opere alio loco idem doctor : < Impugnatur, > inquit, < Paulus, eI. videt legem carnis suae repugnantem legi mentis suæ , et captivantem se in lege peccati;
passages.english: If the impulse of this resisting [force] were loosened, to what unclean things would it not turn aside? Into what precipices would it not drag and hurl [us]? But now, what is more pressing: see, not some Jew or other, as you claim, but, according to blessed Ambrose, the apostle Paul says of himself, "I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind, and taking me captive in the law of sin." Again in the same work, in another place, the same teacher says: "Paul is assailed, and sees the law of his flesh fighting against the law of his mind, and taking him captive in the law of sin;

passages.original: a Si te non deseruit qualiscumque saltem sensus humanus, vides quid de concupiscentiae voluptate, hac ipsa cui præbes impudentissimum patrocinium, pronuntiaverit, tui, quod sæpe dicendum est, doctoris testimonio praedicatus, tam memorabilis doctor Ambrosius : quod ea quisque concretus, ea genitalibus visceribus infusus, ea coagulatus in sanguine ; et in pannis, non utique laneis, aut lineis, aut hujuscemodi talibus, qualibus jam nati obvolvuntur infantes, sed pannis vitiatae originis tanquam hæreditariis involutus, prius subeat contagium delictorum, quam vitalis hujus aeris auram spirando percipiat: in quem velut immensum fontem communis et nou desisten- tis alimenti, post occulta spiramenta viscerum maternorum, qui nascitur, funditur ;
passages.english: If at least some ordinary human sense has not deserted you, you see what was pronounced concerning the pleasure of concupiscence — this very thing for which you provide a most shameless defence — by so memorable a teacher, Ambrose, praised, as must often be said, by the testimony of your own teacher: that by it each person is formed, by it poured into the genital organs, by it curdled in blood; and wrapped in swaddling clothes, not of wool or linen or anything of that kind, in which infants are wrapped once born, but in the clothes of a corrupted origin, as if inherited, he undergoes the contagion of sins before he takes in by breathing the breath of this life-giving air: into which, as into a boundless fountain of common and unfailing nourishment, he who is born is poured out after the hidden passages of the mother's womb;
passages.notes: 'Your own teacher' refers to Pelagius, who praised Ambrose (inferred from usage). Leading 'a' is a stray mark.

passages.original: 48. Merito idem beatus Joannes, etiam ipse, sicut et martyr Cyprianus (Epist. 6t, ad Fidum) , circumcisionem carnis in signo præceptam commendat esse Baptismatis. « Et vide quomodo Judæus, > inquit , i circumcisionem non differt propter comminationem, quia omnis anima quæcumque non fuerit circumcisa die octavo, exterminabitur de populo suo > (Gen.
passages.english: 48. Rightly the same blessed John, he too, just as the martyr Cyprian also does (Letter 64, to Fidus), teaches that the circumcision of the flesh was commanded as a sign of baptism. "And see how the Jew," he says, "does not put off circumcision, because of the threat that every soul whatever that has not been circumcised on the eighth day shall be cut off from its people" (Gen.
passages.notes: "Epist. 6t" read as Epist. 64 (Cyprian's letter to Fidus). The scripture reference continues in the following passage (Gen. 17:14).

passages.original: quæ vestra quingue facitis argumenta, contendentes nullum istorum quinque verum esse posse, nisi falsum sit trahere nascentes originale peccatum : tamen hoc ipsum, quod his quinque argumentis auferre conamini, sic ille ubi opus est, in suis sermonibus ponit, ut cuivis satis eluceat, quid catholica veritas soleat prædicare, quid profana novitas conetur evertere. An forte ipsum quoque Ambrosium scisse ac docuisse dubitabis, Deum esse hominum conditorem, et animæ et corporis ? Audi ergo quid dicat in libro de Philosophia contra Platonem philosophuln , qui hominum animas revolvi in bestias asseverat, et animarum tantummodo Deum opinatur auctorem, corpora autem diis minoribus facienda decernit. Ergo sanctus Ambrosius , c Miror, > inquit, « tantum philosophum, quomodo animam, cui potestatem conferendæ immortalitatis attribuit, in noctuis includat, aut ranulis, feritate quoque induat bestiarum : cum in Timaeo eam Dei opus esse memoraverit, inter immortalia a Deo factam ;
passages.english: the five arguments you make, contending that none of these five can be true unless it is false that those being born contract original sin; yet this very thing, which you try to take away by these five arguments, he sets down in his sermons where it is needed in such a way that it is clear enough to anyone what catholic truth is accustomed to preach and what profane novelty is trying to overturn. Or will you perhaps doubt that Ambrose too knew and taught that God is the maker of human beings, of both soul and body? Hear then what he says in the book On Philosophy against the philosopher Plato, who asserts that human souls are turned back into beasts, and holds God to be the author of souls alone, but decrees that bodies are to be made by lesser gods. So holy Ambrose says: "I wonder how so great a philosopher shuts up the soul, to which he attributed the power of conferring immortality, in owls or little frogs, and also clothes it in the savagery of beasts, when in the Timaeus he recorded that it is the work of God, made by God among the immortal things;
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence; its opening clause depends on the preceding text.

passages.original: Dei autem gratia sic nos in hoc corruptibili corpore adjuvat dimicantes; ut non desit propter quod exaudiat veniam postulantes. Istam super nos Dei misericordiam, vobis necessariam non putatis; quoniam ex eo numero estis, de quibus in Psalmo dictum est, Qui confidunt in virtute tua (Psal. XLVIII, 7). Sed quanto melius audimus Ambrosium in libro de Fuga saeculi dicentem: « Frequens nobis de effugiendo isto saeculo est sermo : atque utinam quant facilis sermo, tam cautus et sollicitus affectus. Sed quod pejus est, frequenter irrepit terrenarum illecebra cupiditatum , et vanitatum offusio mentem occupat, ut quod studeas vitare, hoc cogites, animoque volvas. Quod cavere difficile est homini, exuereautem impossibile.
passages.english: And the grace of God so helps us as we fight in this corruptible body that there is no lack of reason for him to hear us when we ask for pardon. This mercy of God over us you do not think necessary for you, since you are of the number of those of whom it is said in the Psalm, "Who trust in your strength" (Ps. 48:7). But how much better we listen to Ambrose, saying in the book On Flight from the World: "We often speak of fleeing this world; and would that our disposition were as wary and careful as our speech is easy. But what is worse, the allurement of earthly desires often creeps in, and an outpouring of vanities takes hold of the mind, so that what you strive to avoid, you think about and turn over in your mind. This is difficult for a person to guard against, and impossible to put off.
passages.notes: The psalm quotation (Ps. 48:7 Vulgate) reads "in virtute sua" (their own strength) in the Vulgate; the text here has "tua" (your), possibly an error.

passages.original: LXXXIII, 6 ) : « Itemque idem ipse in libro de Sacramento regenerationis : « Quis igitur est, > inquit, « qui carne utitur ad operandum, nisi anima? Ergo princeps et domina carnis naturaliter anima est, quae domare carnem debet et regere. Ideoque Spiritus sancti fulta praesidio, dicit in Psalmo, Non timebo quid faciat mihi caro > (Psal. LV,5). « Ipsa eadem dicit in Paulo, Sed castigo corpus meum, et servituti redigo » ( ICor. IX, 2i7). « Castigat ergo Paulus quod ipsius est, non quod ipse est. Aliud enim quod ipsius, aliud quod ipse est. Castigatquod ipsius est, ut mortem in se lascivise corporalis justus opcretur. > Numquid sanctus Ambrosius quando ista dicebat, non cum vitiis confligebat? non vitia vincebat? non exercitum quemdam variarum cupiditatum intra semeL ipsum, tanquam Christi miles egregius debellabat? non corpus proprium castigabal?Numquid nun supcratis et oppugnatis diaboli operibus , opus Dci cum opere Dei, hoc est, anima cum carne pacem justitiæ requirebat, ut non in sua virtute confidens, sed sicut ait, « Spiritus sancti fulta praesidio diceret, Non timebo quid faciat mihi caro ?
passages.english: 83:6): "And likewise the same man in the book On the Sacrament of Regeneration: 'Who then is it,' he says, 'that uses the flesh in order to act, if not the soul? Therefore the soul is by nature the ruler and mistress of the flesh, which ought to tame and govern the flesh. And so, supported by the protection of the Holy Spirit, it says in the Psalm, I will not fear what flesh may do to me' (Ps. 55:5). 'The same soul says in Paul, But I chastise my body and bring it into subjection' (1 Cor. 9:27). 'So Paul chastises what is his, not what he is. For what is his is one thing, what he is is another. He chastises what is his, so that as a just man he may bring about in himself the death of bodily wantonness.'" Was holy Ambrose, when he said these things, not in conflict with vices? Was he not conquering vices? Was he not subduing within himself, like an outstanding soldier of Christ, a kind of army of various desires? Was he not chastising his own body? When the works of the devil had been overcome and assaulted, was he not seeking the peace of justice for the work of God with the work of God, that is, for the soul with the flesh, so that, not trusting in his own strength but, as he says, "supported by the protection of the Holy Spirit," he might say, I will not fear what flesh may do to me?
passages.notes: Begins with the tail of a psalm reference (Ps. 83:6) from the preceding passage.

passages.original: Si avaritia prostrata est, exsurgit libido : si libido compressa est, succedit ambitio : si ambitio contempta est, ira exasperat, inflat' superbia, vinolentia invitat, invidia concordiam rumpit, amicitiam zelus abscindit. Cogeris maledicere, quod divina lex prohibet; compelleris jurare, quod non licet. Tot persecutiones animus quotidie patitur, tot periculis pectus urgetur, et delectat hic inter diaboli gladios diu stare, cum magis concupiscendum sit et optandum, ad Christum subveniente velocius morte properare. » Absit autem ut sanctum Cyprianum aut avarum existimemus fuisse, quia cum avaritia; aut impudicum, quia cum impudicitia ; aut iræ subditum, quia cum ira; aut ambitiosum , quia cum ambilione; aut carnalem , quia cum carnalibus vitiis;
passages.english: If avarice is laid low, lust rises up; if lust is suppressed, ambition takes its place; if ambition is despised, anger provokes, pride puffs up, drunkenness entices, envy breaks concord, jealousy cuts friendship apart. You are driven to curse, which the divine law forbids; you are forced to swear, which is not permitted. So many persecutions the mind suffers daily, by so many dangers the heart is pressed, and yet it pleases [us] to stand here long among the swords of the devil, when it should rather be desired and wished for to hasten to Christ with the help of a swifter death." But far be it from us to think that holy Cyprian was either avaricious, because [he fought] with avarice; or unchaste, because with unchastity; or subject to anger, because with anger; or ambitious, because with ambition; or carnal, because with carnal vices;

passages.original: Nunc ergo ne tui stomachi follis indigesta maledictorum cruditate rumpa, tur, in hunc evome, si audes, calumniosas tuas vanitates, et insanias mendaces. Ad hæc, inquit, noa vitia naturæ nostræ propellit instinctus. Quæ ista natura est? Numquid gens tcnebrarum, quam Manichæorum fabula inducit? Absit. Catholicus loquitur, insignis Ecclesiarum doctor loquitur, Hilarius loquitur. Nostra ergo natura est primi hominis prævaricatione vitiata, non ab alia natura ulla divisione separanda, sed ipsa sananda : cui diabolum a nobis constitui calumniaris auclorcm, dum tu ei Christum invides salvatorem , et ejus hic vitam, ita ut sine ullo sit omnino peccato, perfectam duci posse contendis.
passages.english: Now then, so that the bellows of your stomach may not burst from the undigested rawness of your curses, vomit out on him, if you dare, your slanderous vanities and lying ravings. "To these vices," he says, "the impulse of our nature drives [us]." What nature is this? Is it the race of darkness which the fable of the Manichees introduces? Far from it. A catholic speaks, a distinguished teacher of the churches speaks, Hilary speaks. Our nature, then, has been vitiated by the transgression of the first man; it is not to be separated off from some other nature by a division, but is itself to be healed. You falsely claim that we make the devil its author, while you begrudge it Christ as saviour, and contend that its life can be led here to perfection, so as to be wholly without any sin.

passages.original: 32, Dicit beatus Ambrosius, unum solum hominem mediatorem Dei et bominum, eo quod sit natus ex virgine, nec senserit nascendo peccatum, gcnerationis obnoxiæ vinculis non teneri. Omnes autem homines sub peccato nasci, quorum ipse ortus in vitio est: quia concupiscentiæ voluptate concreti, prius subirent contagia delictorum, quam vitalem de boc aere spiritum ducerent.
passages.english: 32. Blessed Ambrose says that one man alone, the mediator of God and men, because he was born of a virgin and did not experience sin in being born, is not held by the bonds of a liable generation; but that all human beings are born under sin, whose very origin is in fault, because, being formed by the pleasure of concupiscence, they underwent the contagion of sins before they drew the breath of life from this air.

passages.original: cernentes flagitium, sed intentionem mentis, non sicut oportet, ne illo incidat, inde avertentes, aut si inciderit inde rapientes. De hac lege peccati, quæ alio modo etiam peccatum vocatur, quæ repugnat legi munUs, de qua multa beatus dixit Ambrosius, attestantur etiam sancii, Cyprianus, Hilarius, Cregorius, aliique quam plurimi. Qui ergo generatur is Adam, regenerandus in Christo, mortuus in Adam, vivificandus in Christo, ideo peccato est obstrictus on linis, quia de malo nascitur, quo caro concupiscit adversus spiritum ;
passages.english: not indeed committing the shameful deed, but not turning the attention of the mind away from there as they ought, so as not to fall into it, or, if it has fallen in, snatching it away from there. Of this law of sin, which in another way is also called sin, which fights against the law of the mind, and about which blessed Ambrose said much, the saints Cyprian, Hilary, Gregory and very many others also bear witness. Whoever then is begotten in Adam, to be regenerated in Christ, dead in Adam, to be made alive in Christ, is bound by sin from his origin because he is born from the evil by which the flesh lusts against the spirit;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "munUs" = mentis, "is Adam" = in Adam, "on linis" = originis ("from his origin").

passages.original: 54) : Quia si tales judices, quales definivit, unde hoc dixisti, Sallustius, quæreretis ; sancto Ambrosio et coepiscopis ejus, qui de hac re ab odio vestri vel amicitia, vel ira, vel quod tu non posuisti, sed Sallustius posuit (De Conjuratione Catilinæ, in oratione Cæsaris), misericordia pro vobls, vel contra vos, vacuum pectus habuerunt , quando de bac re veras tranquillasque sententias protulerunt, utique cedcretis 1.
passages.english: 54): Because if you were seeking judges such as Sallust defined, from whom you took this saying, you would surely yield to holy Ambrose and his fellow bishops, who in this matter had a heart free of hatred toward you, or friendship, or anger, or (what you did not put but Sallust did, De Coniuratione Catilinae, in Caesar's speech) pity, whether for you or against you, when they delivered true and calm judgements on this matter.
passages.notes: Begins with the end of a cross-reference (Book 2, n. 54) from the preceding text.

passages.original: Unde Pclagius, quod supra commemoravi cos qui dicunt, infantes, etiamsi non baptizentur, habere vitam æternam, i in ecclesiastico judicio (a) nisi damnasset, damnatus exisset. Qua justitia, quæso, a regno Dei, a vita Dei alienatur imago Dui, in nullo transgressa legem Dei? Nonne audis quemadmodum detestatur Apostolus quosdam, quos dicit alienatos a vita Dei per ignorantiam quæ est in illis propter cecitatem cordis eorum (Ephes. IV, 18)? Tenebitur hac sententia non baptizatus parvulus, an non tenebitur? Si dixeritis, Non tenebitur : evangelica veritate, lingua etiam Pelagii teste, vincemini atque puniemini. Ubi est enim vita Dei, nisi in regno Dei, quo nisi renati ex aqua et spiritu, intrare non possunt (Joan. III, 5)? Si autem dixeritis, Tenebitur: fatemini poenam, culpam dicite;
passages.english: Hence Pelagius, had he not condemned in the ecclesiastical court, as I mentioned above, those who say that infants, even if they are not baptized, have eternal life, would have come out condemned. By what justice, I ask, is the image of God, which has in no respect transgressed the law of God, estranged from the kingdom of God, from the life of God? Do you not hear how the Apostle denounces certain people whom he describes as estranged from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them because of the blindness of their heart (Eph. 4:18)? Will the unbaptized little one be held by this sentence, or will he not? If you say, "He will not be held," you will be defeated and punished by the truth of the Gospel, with even Pelagius' own tongue as witness. For where is the life of God, if not in the kingdom of God, which none can enter unless they are reborn of water and the Spirit (John 3:5)? But if you say, "He will be held," [then] you admit a penalty: name the guilt;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected (e.g. 'Pclagius', 'cos', 'Dui' for 'Dei', 'cecitatem'). The stray 'i' and the '(a)' footnote mark are omitted. The passage ends mid-sentence, continuing in the following text.

passages.original: Ridiculum est autcm, quod mé dicis, < Epicuri vias gradientem habenas omnes, quibus cupiditates frenantur, incidere. Y Quid, si ego laudarem corporis voluptatem ? Hoc enim tu satis eloquenter faeis, quod inerudite atque impoliie faciebat Epicurus : quasi propterea sis ejus adversarius, quia diserte dicere non noverat ille , quæ dicis. Rursus , ut sentio, laboraturus es, quomodo te ostendas et laudatorem voluptatis esse, et Epicurcum non esse.
passages.english: But it is ridiculous that you say I, "walking the ways of Epicurus, cut all the reins by which desires are curbed." What if I were praising bodily pleasure? For you do that quite eloquently, which Epicurus did in an unlearned and unpolished way: as if you were his adversary because he did not know how to say eloquently the things you say. Again, as I perceive, you will labour over how to show that you are both a praiser of pleasure and not an Epicurean.

passages.original: et de que item legitur, Si quis indiget sapientia, postulet a Deo (Jacobi i, 5) ? Verum si tu non es Epicureus, qui ex illo aliquam partem in voluptatis laude sumpsisti: quanto minus ego, qui de voluptate carnis hoc sentio, quod sentit Ambrosius ( Libro de Paradiso , cap. 12, et libro de Philosophia, citato supra, lib. 2, nn. 13,15 ); inimicam scilicet esse justitiae, et quod bomo concupiscentiæ voluptate concretus, priusquam nascitur subeat contagia delictorum.
passages.english: and of whom it is likewise read, "If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of God" (James 1:5)? But if you are not an Epicurean, though you have taken some part from him in praising pleasure, how much less am I, who hold about the pleasure of the flesh what Ambrose holds (Book on Paradise, ch. 12, and the book on Philosophy, cited above, book 2, nn. 13, 15): namely that it is hostile to justice, and that a human being, conceived through the pleasure of concupiscence, incurs the contagion of sins before he is born.
passages.notes: "de que" read as "de quo"; "bomo" as "homo".

passages.original: > Hæc ubi didiceris, nescio: jam tamen cernis, ut arbitror, consequens esse ut vera sit virtus, avarorum prudentia, qua excogitant genera lucellorum et avarorum justitia, qua gravium damnorum metu facilius sua nonnunquam contemnunt, quam usurpant aliquid alienum; et avarorum temperantia, qua luxuriae, quoniam sumptuosa est, cohibent appetitum, soloque necessario victu tegumentoque contenti sunt; et avarorum fortitudo, qua, ut ait Horatius, Per maTe pauperiem fugiant, per .axa, per ignes. (Horatius, lib. 1, epist. I, vers. 46.) qua denique cognovimus quosdam irruptione barbarica , ad ea prodenda quæ habebant, nullis hostium tormentis potuisse compelli.
passages.english: Where you learned these things, I do not know; yet you now see, I think, that it follows that the prudence of the avaricious is true virtue, by which they devise kinds of petty profits; and the justice of the avaricious, by which, from fear of heavy losses, they sometimes more readily disregard their own property than seize anything belonging to another; and the temperance of the avaricious, by which they restrain the appetite for luxury, since it is costly, and are content with only necessary food and clothing; and the fortitude of the avaricious, by which, as Horace says, "They flee poverty across the sea, across rocks, through fires" (Horace, Epistles 1.1.46); by which, finally, we have known that certain men, during a barbarian invasion, could not be compelled by any tortures of the enemy to give up what they had.
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected: "maTe" = mare, ".axa" = saxa.

passages.original: Sed volens ostendere, non omnia quæ teguntur, ex peccato erubescenda putari oportere, multum inaniter multa commemoras, quas in nostro corpore naturaliter tecta sunt; quasi post peccatum tecta sint, sicut illi homines, uude inter nos quæstio est, quæ ante peccatum nec pudenda, nec tecta fuerant, post peccatum pudenda texerunt. < BaIbus, > inquis, « apud Tullium cum Cotta vere diligcnterque disseruit > (De Natura deorum, lib. 2). < Unde ob hoc pauca ponis, > ut dicis, < ut oneres pudorem meum, non ea me intellexisse sub magisterio sacræ legis, ad quorum notionem Gentiles solo rationis du.
passages.english: But wishing to show that not everything that is covered should be thought shameful because of sin, you recount at great length and to no purpose many things which are naturally covered in our body, as if they had been covered after sin, in the way that those people, about whom the question between us is, covered after sin as shameful the things which before sin had been neither shameful nor covered. "Balbus," you say, "in Tully, discoursed truly and carefully with Cotta" (On the Nature of the Gods, book 2). "Hence for this reason you set down a few things," as you say, "to burden my modesty, [showing] that I had not understood under the teaching of the sacred law things to the knowledge of which the Gentiles were able to arrive under the guidance of reason alone.
passages.notes: The sentence runs into the text after the passage ("du-/cta pervenire"); translated as completed there.

passages.original: Frustra igitur testimonio Stoicorum juvandam putasti tuam esse susceptam, non sane illis amicam, qui nullam particulam boni humani in corporis voluptate posuerunt. Denique clegerunt in pecoribus potius quam in hominibus, quod tu facis, laudare libidines. Eorum quippe opinioni convenienter ait quodam loco Tullius, se non putare idem esse arietis et Publii Africani bonum. Qua magis sententia te oportuit admoneri , quid de humana libidine sentire deberes.
passages.english: In vain, then, did you think that your cause should be helped by the testimony of the Stoics, which is certainly not friendly to them, since they placed no particle of human good in the pleasure of the body. In short, they chose to praise lusts in cattle rather than in human beings, as you do. Indeed, in keeping with their opinion, Tully says in one place that he does not think the good of a ram and of Publius Africanus to be the same. By this judgment you should rather have been reminded what you ought to think about human lust.
passages.notes: "tuam esse susceptam" is awkward; probably "tuam causam susceptam" ("the cause you took up"); "non sane illis amicam" seemingly means your cause is not friendly to the Stoics.

passages.original: Sed si talibus litteris ut aliquid agamus, placet, quia et in ipsis reperiuntur nonnulla vestigia veritatis; interim quæ ipse posuisti, nihil adversus nos valere, puto quod jam debeas confiteri. Vide nunc utrum ista quæ dicam, non evertant assertionem tuam. In libro tertio de Republica, idem Tullius hominem dicit, < non ut a matre, sed ut a noverca natura editum in vitam, corpore nudo, fragili, et infirmo; animo autem anxio ad molestias, humili ad timores, molli ad labores, prono ad libidines : in quo tamen inesset tanquam obrutus quidam divinus ignis ingenii et menlis.
passages.english: But if it pleases [you] that we deal with such writings, since in them too some traces of truth are found, meanwhile I think you ought now to admit that the things you yourself set down have no force against us. See now whether the things I shall say do not overturn your assertion. In the third book of the Republic the same Tully says that man was brought forth into life by nature "not as by a mother but as by a stepmother, with a body naked, frail and weak, and with a mind anxious toward troubles, abject toward fears, soft toward labours, prone to lusts; in which nevertheless there was, as it were buried, a certain divine fire of intellect and mind."

passages.original: Obsecro te, non sit honestior philosophia Gentium, quam nostra Christiana, qux una est vera philosophia, quandoquidem studium vel amor sapientiæ significatur hoc nomine. Vide enim quid ill Hortensii dialogo I dicat Tullius; quæ magis verba te delectaro debuerant, quam Balbi Stoicorum partes agentis : quæ licet vera, tamen de parte hominis inferiore, hoc est, de corpore fuerunt, ct te nihil adjuvare potuerunt. Vide quid iste pro vivacitate mentis contra voluptatem corporis dicat.
passages.english: I beg you, let the philosophy of the Gentiles not be more honourable than our Christian [philosophy], which is the one true philosophy, since by this name the pursuit or love of wisdom is signified. For see what Tully says in the dialogue Hortensius; words which ought to have delighted you more than those of Balbus playing the part of the Stoics, which, though true, were about the inferior part of man, that is, the body, and could not help you at all. See what he says on behalf of the vigour of the mind against the pleasure of the body.
passages.notes: "ill Hortensii dialogo I" read as "in Hortensio dialogo".

passages.original: Ne scilicet in ipsa de voluptate quæstione unde tccuin agimus, honestiores philosophite obruerent, quos Cicero propter ipsam honestatem tanquam consularcs philosophos nuncupavit; et ipsi Stoici maximc inimicissimi voluptatis, quorum testimonium I ex persona Balbi apud Ciceronem disputantis, verum quidem, sed quod libi prorsus nihil prodesset, interponendum putasti (Supra, n. 58). Quod autem nullum hominis bonum censeant corporis voluptatem cupiens abscondere, nulla de quaestione morali nomina et dogmata philosophorum , quod maxime ad rem pertinebat, si aliquid de philosophis probandum fuit, commemorare voluisti.
passages.english: [You did so] lest, namely, in the very question about pleasure on which we are dealing with you, the more honourable philosophers should overwhelm you, whom Cicero, because of that very honourableness, called as it were consular philosophers; and the Stoics themselves, the most hostile of all to pleasure, whose testimony from the person of Balbus disputing in Cicero, true indeed but of no use whatever to you, you thought should be inserted (above, n. 58). But because they hold that bodily pleasure is no good of man, you, wishing to hide this, chose to mention no names and doctrines of philosophers on any moral question, which was most to the point, if anything was to be proved from the philosophers.

passages.original: Nam cum multa quæ videmus et gemimus, de hominum vanitate atque infelicitate dixisset : « Ex quibus humanae, > inquit, < vitæ erroribus et ærumnis fit, ut interdum veteres illi, sive vates, sive in sacris initiisque tradendis divinae mentis interpretes, qui nos ob aliqua scelera suscepta in vita superiore, poenarum luendarum causa natos esse dixerunt, aliquid vidisse videantur : verumque sit illud quod est apud Aristotelem, simili nos affectos esse supplicio, atque eos qui quondam, cum in prædonum Etruscorum manus incidissent, crudelitate excogitata necabantur, quorum corpora viva cum mortuis, adversa adversis accommodata, quam aptissi- me colligabantur;
passages.english: For when he had said many things, which we see and lament, about the vanity and unhappiness of human beings, he says: "From these errors and hardships of human life it comes about that at times those ancients, whether seers or interpreters of the divine mind in handing down sacred rites and initiations, who said that we were born to pay penalties for some crimes committed in a former life, seem to have seen something; and that saying in Aristotle is true, that we are afflicted with a punishment like that of those who once, when they had fallen into the hands of Etruscan pirates, were put to death with contrived cruelty: their living bodies were bound as tightly as possible to dead ones, face fitted to face;

passages.original: Quid, quod istam pulcherrimam famulam tuam, quam me pudet assidue vel vituperando nominare, te autem prædicare non pudct, < commendatiorem fieri putas, quod ei serviunt, ut ardentius excitetur, etiam cæteræ corporis partes, sive oculi videntes ad concupiscendum, sive alia membra in osculis et amplexibus? > Aures quoque hominis quomodo ei subderes invenisti, et erexisti ejus vetustissimum quidem, sed plane gloriosissimum titulum, commemorans quod in expositione Consiliorum suorum Tullius posuit : < Quia cum vinolenti adolescentes tibiarum etiam cantu , ut fit, instincti, mnlicris pudice fores frangerent; admonuisse tibicinam, ut spondeum caneret, Pythagoras dicitur : quod cum illa fecisset, tarditatc modorum ct gravitate cantus illorum furentem petulantiam resedisse 1.
passages.english: What of the fact that you think this most beautiful handmaid of yours, whom I am ashamed to name constantly even in censure, but you are not ashamed to extol, "becomes more commendable because the other parts of the body also serve her so that she may be more ardently aroused, whether the eyes seeing so as to desire, or other members in kisses and embraces"? You have found how to subject even a person's ears to her, and you have raised up her very ancient, but plainly most glorious, title, recalling what Tully set down in the exposition of his Counsels: "When drunken young men, excited also, as happens, by the music of pipes, were breaking down the doors of a chaste woman, Pythagoras is said to have advised the pipe-girl to play a spondee; and when she had done so, by the slowness of the measures and the gravity of the song their raging wantonness subsided."
passages.notes: "famulam" refers to concupiscence/lust. The trailing "1" is a footnote mark.

passages.original: Non cst enim quomodo faciat quod non !icct, quando licct quidquid libct, quia bonum est quod naturaliter libet. Si crgo adsunt, voluptatibus perfruatur : si autem non adsunt, ipsis carum cogitationibus, sicut Epicuro visum cist, oblectetur, et erit sine peccato, nec se ullo fraudabit bono : nec cujuscumque doctrinae opinionibus resistat naturalibus motibus, scd, sicut ait Hortensius, < tunc obsequatur naturæ, cum sine magistro senserit quid natura dcsideret » (Ciceronis dialogus, cui nomen Hortensius).
passages.english: For there is no way for him to do what is not permitted, when whatever pleases is permitted, because what naturally pleases is good. If, then, [pleasures] are at hand, let him enjoy them to the full; but if they are not at hand, let him delight in the very thoughts of them, as Epicurus held, and he will be without sin and will not cheat himself of any good; nor let him resist natural impulses on the opinions of any doctrine, but, as Hortensius says, "let him obey nature when, without a teacher, he has perceived what nature desires" (Cicero's dialogue called Hortensius).
passages.notes: Ironic: Augustine is drawing out the consequences of Julian's view.

passages.original: Ego autem ( quia libcrorum procreandorum causa uxores esse ducendas , honestas consentit humana, quolibet modo libidini ccdat infirmitas), prætcr fidem quam sibi debent conjuges, ne fiant adulteria, et prolcm cujus gcnerandac causa sexus terque miscendus est , adverti etiam tcriium bonum quod esse in conjugibus debet, maxime pertinentibus ad populum Dei, quod milii visum est esse aliquod sacramentum, ne divortium fiat vcl ab ca conjuge quaa non potest parere, vel sicut fccisse Cato perhibetur (Plutarch. in ejus Vita, ct Lucan. lib. 2), ne ab eo viro qui pluresnon vult suscipere filius, alteri fetanda tradatar (De Nuptiis et Concupiscentia, lib. 1, n. ii. Propter hoc in i!!o qnod secundum Evangelium con - .
passages.english: But I (since human decency agrees that wives are to be married for the sake of begetting children, however much weakness may yield to lust), besides the faith which spouses owe each other, so that adulteries may not occur, and the offspring for the sake of whose begetting the two sexes are to be joined, have also noticed a third good which ought to be in spouses, especially those belonging to the people of God, which seemed to me to be a kind of sacrament: that divorce should not take place, either from a wife who cannot bear children, or, as Cato is reported to have done (Plutarch in his Life, and Lucan book 2), that she should not be handed over to another to be made fruitful by a husband who does not want to raise more children (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 1, n. 11). For this reason, in that which according to the Gospel I called a mar-
passages.notes: Many scanning errors silently corrected (e.g. liberorum, praeter, prolem, generandae, uterque, tertium, mihi, vel, quae, fecisse, plures non, filios, fetanda tradatur, illo quod). 'consentit humana' read as 'honestas ... humana' (human decency); the clause is somewhat awkward. The final sentence breaks off mid-word ('con-/jugium', marriage), continued in the following passage.

passages.original: quia 1 erunt et corpore spirituales , quando seminatum corpus animale, resurget corpus spirituale (! Cor. xv, 44) : et recte adhuc intelliguntur ea parte captivi sub lege peccati, qux; desiderio. rum, quibus non consentiunt, motibus subjacet. Hinc factum est ut sic ista intelligerem, quemadmodum intellexit Hilarius, Gregorius, Ambrosius, et cæteri Ecclesiæ sancti notique doctores , qui et ipsum Apostolum adversus carnales concupiscentias quas habero nolebat, et tamen habebat, strenue condixisse, eumdemque conflictum suum illis suis verbis contestatum fuisse senserunt (Supra, lib.
passages.english: because they will be spiritual in body too, when the body sown as an animal body rises again as a spiritual body (1 Cor. 15:44); and they are still rightly understood to be captives under the law of sin in that part which is subject to the movements of desires to which they do not consent. Hence it came about that I understood these things as Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other holy and well-known doctors of the Church understood them, who held that the Apostle himself strenuously fought against the carnal desires which he did not wish to have and yet had, and that he bore witness to this same conflict of his in those words of his (Above, book
passages.notes: The passage begins mid-sentence and ends mid-reference ('book 2, chapters 3 and 4' continues in the following context). 'condixisse' (literally 'declared/agreed') is taken in context as 'fought against'; perhaps read 'contradixisse' (spoke against). Scanning errors corrected (quae, desideriorum, habere).
